title: Agreement With Yourself Is Not Reliability
summary: A reliability figure for an LLM-annotated corpus almost always has the same shape. You pick a model, write a prompt, run it on three thousand tweets three times, and report a Fleiss' kappa between the runs. The number is high — usually...
body:
A reliability figure for an LLM-annotated corpus almost always has the same shape. You pick a model, write a prompt, run it on three thousand tweets three times, and report a Fleiss' $\kappa$ between the runs. The number is high — usually well north of 0.9 — and it goes in the methods section as the project's inter-rater agreement. A September 2026 paper by Thomas Reiter, Christoph Kern, Fedor Miasnikov, Sofiia Nikolenko, Rob Chew, Stephanie Eckman, and Frauke Kreuter, accepted to the 3rd Workshop on Uncertainty-Aware NLP at EMNLP 2026, makes the methodological case that the number is not what the social scientist wanted.

The paper's own figures sharpen the point. Across seven LLMs, three replication runs, and three thousand tweets labelled for offensive language and hate speech, the median Fleiss' $\kappa$ *within* a fixed task design is 0.91. Across twelve plausible task designs applied to the *same tweets*, the median pairwise Cohen's $\kappa$ is 0.76. The two numbers describe different objects: the first is repeatability under a fixed instrument; the second is reliability across instruments. On downstream prevalence estimation the gap is not a rounding error. The variance of the estimated prevalence inflates by a factor of 76.7 for offensive-language labels and 110.6 for hate-speech labels, relative to the sampling variance that gets reported under the "just use the one prompt" convention.

## Why this matters now

The LLM-as-annotator literature has swung hard toward "validate on each task" since Pangakis, Wolken and Fasching's 2023 argument in that direction, but validation has been operationalised almost entirely as agreement with a human gold set, not as stability across alternative design choices that a diligent coder could have picked. Christoph Kern and Frauke Kreuter had already made the point in the human-annotation case in 2023: five randomly assigned experimental conditions of the same annotation instrument produced statistically significant differences in hate-speech prevalence estimates, in downstream model performance, and in model learning curves. The April 2026 proposal by Jingyuan Liu — Inter-Prompt Reliability, IPR — formalised the same complaint for LLM annotators and proposed a pairwise-agreement metric across semantically equivalent prompts. Five months later Reiter et al. give the first careful end-to-end measurement under that framing, and the picture is not favourable to current practice.

## The core idea, developed properly

Generalizability theory is the right scaffolding. In a G-study, the observed score $X_{p r}$ of person $p$ by rater $r$ admits a variance decomposition
$$\sigma^2(X) = \sigma^2_p + \sigma^2_r + \sigma^2_{p r} + \sigma^2_e,$$
where $\sigma^2_p$ is systematic variance across objects of measurement (the tweets), $\sigma^2_r$ is systematic variance across the instrument (the rater), $\sigma^2_{p r}$ is the item-by-rater interaction, and $\sigma^2_e$ is residual noise. The reliability coefficient one reports is a ratio of $\sigma^2_p$ to the total variance that remains after averaging over the irrelevant facets; a different facet structure gives a different coefficient, and this is why the choice of what counts as a "facet" is a modelling decision, not a measurement.

An LLM-annotation pipeline has facets that are not just "raters." Call a *design* $d$ the tuple (model, prompt phrasing, output-extraction rule, aggregation rule) and let $k$ index a replication under fixed $d$. The realised label $\hat{y}(p, d, k)$ decomposes as
$$\sigma^2(\hat{y}) \;=\; \sigma^2_p \;+\; \sigma^2_d \;+\; \sigma^2_{p d} \;+\; \sigma^2_{k \mid d},$$
with the last term capturing the temperature-induced run-to-run variance under fixed $d$. The median Fleiss' $\kappa$ of 0.91 that Reiter et al. report is an estimate of $\sigma^2_{k \mid d}$ relative to $\sigma^2_p$: it says that for a given $d$, your labels are almost as reliable as a highly trained panel would be. The median Cohen's $\kappa$ of 0.76 across designs is an estimate of $\sigma^2_d + \sigma^2_{p d}$ relative to $\sigma^2_p$, and it is where the uncertainty lives.

The move from reliability to a downstream *measurement* — a prevalence, a share, a coefficient in a regression on the labels — makes the asymmetry sharper. For a corpus of $n$ items and fixed design $d$, the prevalence estimator $\hat{\pi}_d$ has sampling variance $\pi_d (1 - \pi_d) / n$, which for $\pi \approx 0.1$ and $n = 3000$ is about $3 \cdot 10^{-5}$. The *design-induced* variance of the point estimate across the $D = 12$ reasonable designs is empirically about $76.7 \cdot \pi (1 - \pi) / n$ for offensive-language labels and $110.6$ times that for hate speech. A frequentist interval built from the sampling-variance term alone understates the uncertainty of the construct's prevalence by roughly a factor of $\sqrt{110} \approx 10.5$ — an interval claimed as $\pm 1.1$ percentage points is actually $\pm 11$.

Adding replications of the same design does not help. The relevant generalizability coefficient for a single-design pipeline is
$$G \;=\; \frac{\sigma^2_p}{\sigma^2_p \;+\; \sigma^2_d \;+\; \sigma^2_e / K},$$
and $K \to \infty$ leaves $\sigma^2_d$ intact. The only ways to shrink it are to average over designs explicitly or to narrow the admissible design space.

## A concrete anchor

The arithmetic is more intuitive in miniature. Suppose true hate-speech prevalence in your corpus is $\pi = 0.08$, that $n = 3000$, and that you have run $D = 12$ prompt variants with three replications each. A one-percentage-point design-wise standard deviation of the point estimate — well inside what Reiter et al. observe — puts the between-design variance at $10^{-4}$. The within-design-across-replications variance is at most a few times $10^{-6}$. A naive aggregation that picks "the" prompt and reports $\hat{\pi} \pm 1.96 \sqrt{\hat{\pi}(1 - \hat{\pi})/n}$ will quote $\pm 1.0$ percentage points when the design-aware interval is closer to $\pm 2.3$. The gap is the cost of treating one facet of variance as if it were the whole.

```python
import numpy as np

def design_aware_interval(labels_by_design, alpha=0.05):
    """labels_by_design: dict[design_name -> np.ndarray of 0/1 labels on the same n items]"""
    n = next(iter(labels_by_design.values())).shape[0]
    prevs = np.array([L.mean() for L in labels_by_design.values()])
    pi_hat = prevs.mean()
    v_within = np.mean([p * (1 - p) / n for p in prevs])      # sampling, averaged
    v_between = prevs.var(ddof=1)                              # instrument facet
    z = 1.96
    naive = (pi_hat - z * np.sqrt(v_within),
             pi_hat + z * np.sqrt(v_within))
    aware = (pi_hat - z * np.sqrt(v_within + v_between),
             pi_hat + z * np.sqrt(v_within + v_between))
    return pi_hat, naive, aware
```

Two things are worth noticing. First, the between-design variance you compute is a function of the catalogue of designs you considered, which is a prior. A lazy catalogue of near-identical rewordings will deflate $v_{\text{between}}$; a catalogue that enumerates plausibly admissible alternatives will inflate it. Second, nothing in this construction uses the model's confidence head. Reiter et al. explicitly check, and the confidence scores produced by the LLMs they test do not resolve the sensitivity.

## When this is the right diagnosis

Design sensitivity is not a universal LLM pathology. On strictly knowledge-anchored tasks — question answering against a fixed key, named-entity extraction with a tight ontology — Liu's IPR analysis finds relatively high prompt-to-prompt agreement; the numbers degrade on *interpretive* tasks such as what counts as offensive, what counts as a frame, what counts as a disclosure of symptoms. The generalizability framing makes this expected. When the object of measurement is pinned down by a lexical criterion, a change of design perturbs the function $f_d(\cdot)$ only slightly; when the object requires judgement, it is a genuinely different function. The relevant question for a working project is not "do LLMs agree with themselves" but "does my target construct behave like TREC relevance or like hate speech."

Two concrete diagnostics follow. Both are cheap to run.

A repeatability probe: same model, same prompt, three temperature-zero runs and three temperature-0.7 runs, Fleiss' $\kappa$. A low number here means replications are noisy and more of them will help.

A design-sensitivity probe: hold the corpus fixed, pre-register three to five semantically equivalent prompt variants and at least two model families, run once each, compute Cohen's $\kappa$ between designs and the between-design variance of any downstream statistic you care about. A low number here means replication does not help; what helps is either averaging across designs explicitly or restricting the construct until it stops behaving interpretively.

## Limits and open questions

The G-theory framing clarifies the right questions, not the answers.

What counts as a *reasonable* design is a modelling choice. Reiter et al.'s twelve designs are a curated catalogue intended to feel admissible to a working annotator — not a random sample from the space of possible prompts. A sensitivity analysis that strictly restricts the design space, say to prompts mechanically generated from the same codebook, will show a smaller $\sigma^2_d$ than one that admits paraphrases. The diagnosis depends on the prior over designs, and the paper makes this clear, but it is the step the social-science reader has to do themselves, because the prior is a substantive claim about which instrument versions are interchangeable *for their construct*.

The item-by-design interaction can be large and consequential. Pal, Ahuja, Khanuja, Gautam and Choudhury's "Hidden Measurement Error in LLM Pipelines" (arXiv:2604.11581) reports that a few items are robust to prompt perturbation while others move substantially. A corpus-averaged G-coefficient hides this, with the obvious consequence that marginal prevalence can be stable while subgroup estimates are not — exactly the regime where most computational-social-science claims live. The design-aware interval above is a first-moment correction; a defensible subgroup analysis needs a hierarchical model with design-by-subgroup interactions.

Confidence scores and the self-report trap. Nothing in the Reiter et al. data recovers the design-swap variance from the models' own confidences, and this is consistent with the longer calibration literature. The quantity you want is in the empirical distribution of estimates across designs, not in any single run's confidence head.

A fourth caveat is sociological. Kern and Kreuter's 2023 result on human instrument sensitivity has been available for three years, and the measurement-theory literature it draws on is half a century old. The novelty here is not the decomposition but the fact that the field had to be forced to see it when the raters became cheap enough to run twelve ways. If the current round of methodological papers is read as a story about LLMs specifically, rather than as a reminder of what inter-rater reliability was always measuring, the next generation of LLM-annotated prevalence claims will repeat the same category error with the same confidence intervals.

The practical upshot is modest and operational. Report two $\kappa$ values, not one: repeatability under fixed design and reliability across pre-registered design variants. Report a design-aware interval whenever the labels enter a downstream estimand. Pre-register the catalogue of designs you intend to treat as reasonable *before* you look at the first result, so the catalogue is a measurement instrument rather than a post-hoc defence. This is a small change in method sections and a large change in what the numbers mean.

## Further reading

- Thomas Reiter, Christoph Kern, Fedor Miasnikov, Sofiia Nikolenko, Rob Chew, Stephanie Eckman, Frauke Kreuter, *Reliable but Design-Sensitive: Instrument Uncertainty in LLM Annotation*, arXiv:2609.35824, 3rd UncertaiNLP Workshop at EMNLP 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.35824>. The hero paper: 7 models $\times$ 12 designs $\times$ 3 runs $\times$ 3000 tweets, with the within-design and between-design $\kappa$ figures and the prevalence-variance inflation factors.
- Jingyuan Liu, *What Is Actually Being Annotated? Inter-Prompt Reliability as a Measurement Problem in LLM-Based Social Science Labeling*, arXiv:2604.16413, April 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.16413>. The paper that named IPR and proposed a pairwise-agreement metric across equivalent prompts; the pre-registered measurement-theory framing that Reiter et al. then quantify.
- Christoph Kern and Frauke Kreuter, *Annotation Sensitivity: Training Data Collection Methods Affect Model Performance*, Findings of EMNLP 2023. <https://aclanthology.org/2023.findings-emnlp.992/>. The precedent in the human-annotation case — five randomly assigned instrument conditions, significant differences in prevalence estimates and downstream model behaviour — that the 2026 work extends to LLM annotators.
- Nicholas Pangakis, Samuel Wolken, Neil Fasching, *Automated Annotation with Generative AI Requires Validation*, arXiv:2306.00176, 2023. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.00176>. The paper that set the "validate task by task" norm; worth revisiting after Reiter et al. because its notion of validation is not instrument-aware.
- Simone Pal, Ahuja, Khanuja, Gautam, Choudhury, *Hidden Measurement Error in LLM Pipelines Distorts Annotation, Evaluation, and Benchmarking*, arXiv:2604.11581, 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.11581>. The item-level diagnostic — robust items vs. sensitive items — that motivates hierarchical rather than marginal design-aware corrections.
- Emiliano Camuffo, Alessandro Gambardella, Shaghayegh Kazemi, Alex Malachowski, Pankaj Pandey, *Variance-Aware LLM Annotation for Strategy Research: Sources, Diagnostics, and a Protocol for Reliable Measurement*, arXiv:2601.02370, 2026. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.02370>. A protocol-level companion that enumerates five variance sources in LLM annotation and prescribes sampling budgets and reporting rules; a reasonable template for the pre-registration step the Reiter et al. argument implies.
